client: Lately, I’ve just been feeling so empty and unmotivated. Ever since my partner passed away three months ago, everything I used to enjoy feels meaningless. I keep trying to push myself to do things, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions without any real joy. Honestly, I’m not sure if therapy can even help with something like this—it feels like this loss is just too big to overcome.
therapist: I hear how deeply this loss has affected you, and it makes complete sense that activities you once enjoyed might feel hollow right now. Grief can make even simple tasks feel overwhelming—would you be willing to share what a typical day looks like for you now compared to before?

client: Before, my days had a rhythm—I’d wake up, make breakfast with my partner, go to work, and come home to spend time together. Now, I barely get out of bed most mornings. I drag myself through work, and when I come home, the silence feels suffocating. It’s hard to imagine how anything could feel normal again.
therapist: It sounds like the absence of those shared routines has left a profound void in your daily life. What comes up for you when you imagine trying one small, comforting routine—maybe making breakfast just for yourself—even if it feels different now?

client: Just thinking about making breakfast alone makes my chest feel tight. It’s not just about the food—it’s that I can still hear their laughter in the kitchen, you know? Part of me knows I should try, but another part feels like I’d just be pretending things are okay when they’re not.
therapist: Those contrasting feelings—knowing you "should" try while feeling like it would be pretending—show how complex grief can be. Would it feel different if you thought of making breakfast not as moving on, but as a way to honor those memories while caring for yourself in this moment?

client: I never thought about it that way—as an act of honoring instead of moving on. That actually makes me tear up a little. But what if I just start crying in the middle of making eggs? That thought scares me, like I might fall apart completely if I let myself do those familiar things.
therapist: It's completely understandable that tears might come up—in fact, those emotions showing up during familiar routines shows how deeply you cared. What would it feel like to imagine letting the tears come while you cook, knowing they're part of the love you still carry?

client: I guess I've been treating the tears like something to avoid at all costs, like they're dangerous somehow. But if I think about it as love... that changes things. I'm just afraid once I start crying, I won't be able to stop. Like the grief might swallow me whole if I let it out.
therapist: That fear of being overwhelmed by grief makes so much sense—it shows how powerfully love and loss are intertwined for you right now. What if we thought about those tears not as an endless flood, but as waves that naturally rise and fall—would that feel any different to consider?

client: That wave analogy actually helps a little. I grew up near the ocean, so I know waves do come and go... but what if I'm not strong enough to ride them out? Some days it already feels like I'm barely keeping my head above water. Maybe I could try making breakfast one morning when I'm feeling slightly stronger?
therapist: It sounds like the ocean analogy resonates with you, and I admire your willingness to consider trying breakfast on a day when you feel a bit more grounded. What would it feel like to remind yourself that it’s okay to step back if the waves feel too intense, knowing you can always try again when you’re ready?

client: That permission to step back actually makes it feel less scary. I think I've been putting so much pressure on myself to "get better" on some timeline. But I still worry—what if those "stronger days" never come? It's been three months and some days I feel worse than I did at the beginning.
therapist: It's understandable to worry about the timeline of grief—three months can feel like both an eternity and no time at all when your world has changed so deeply. What if we viewed this as less about waiting for "stronger days" and more about noticing the subtle shifts in how you experience this pain over time?

client: That... that actually makes sense. I have noticed some tiny shifts, like last week when I caught myself smiling at a memory instead of immediately crying. But then I felt guilty for smiling at all. It's so confusing—shouldn't I be getting "better" in a straight line instead of this messy back-and-forth?
therapist: Those mixed feelings—the smile followed by guilt—show how grief isn't linear at all, but more like learning to carry love and loss together. Could we explore what it might feel like to see that moment as part of healing rather than something to feel guilty about?

client: I want to believe that smiling isn't betraying their memory, but it still feels wrong somehow. Like if I start feeling even a little bit okay, it means I'm forgetting them or loving them less. The guilt comes so fast I can barely catch my breath.
therapist: It makes so much sense that joy and grief feel tangled together right now—that's often how deep love shows up after loss. What if we slowed down that moment when guilt arises, and explored what your loved one might say about you finding moments of lightness?

client: That question hits me hard. They... they were always the first to make me laugh, even on my darkest days. I can almost hear them saying "Don't stop living just because I did." But then my stomach knots up because that thought makes the loss feel even more real, you know? Like I'm admitting they're really gone.
therapist: It sounds like in that moment, you're holding both their wisdom about continuing to live and the piercing reality of missing them—what would it feel like to make space for both truths at once, as painful as that might be?
